title: Count Number of Rectangles Containing Each Point
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every rectangle per point versus grouping rectangles by height (a small fixed range) and binary searching lengths within each group.

content.title: Count Number of Rectangles Containing Each Point

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a list of axis-aligned rectangles, each with its bottom-left corner at the origin and described by [length, height], and a list of query points, return, for each point, how many of the rectangles contain it (a point is contained if it lies within or on the boundary of a rectangle).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every rectangle starts at the origin","A point (x, y) is contained exactly when some rectangle has length at least x AND height at least y"],["The height range is small and fixed (1 to 100)","Group rectangles by height, and binary search within each height group for widths at least x"]]}

blocks.text: Since every rectangle starts at the origin, a point (x, y) is contained in a rectangle [length, height] exactly when length is at least x and height is at least y. For every query point, count how many rectangles satisfy both conditions.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Overlapping Origin-Anchored Frames Cover a Point
blocks.text: Picture several rectangular frames, all anchored at the same corner (the origin), of varying width and height, and needing to count, for many query points, how many of these frames extend far enough in both directions to cover each point.

blocks.caption: Group rectangles by height (a small, fixed range); binary search widths within each group

blocks.text: Point (2,1) is contained in rectangles [2,3] and [2,5] (2 rectangles); point (1,4) is contained only in [2,5] (1 rectangle). Result: [2, 1].

Before checking every rectangle against every point directly, notice that the height range is small and fixed, letting rectangles be grouped by height, with widths searched efficiently within each group.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A point (x, y) is contained in rectangle [length, height] exactly when length is at least x and height is at least y, since both start at the origin.

Observation 2: Grouping rectangles by their height, and sorting each group's lengths, lets "how many rectangles of THIS height have length at least x" be answered with a single binary search.

Observation 3: For a query point (x, y), the answer is the sum, over every height from y up to the maximum possible height (100), of how many rectangles at that height have length at least x.

Observation 4: Since the height range is small and fixed (at most 100), this sum runs in a small, bounded number of steps, each an O(log n) binary search.
This leads to grouping rectangles by height, sorting lengths within each group, and answering each query by summing binary-search counts across every height at least the point's y-coordinate.
For every query point, check every rectangle directly for containment.

items: For every point (x, y), scan every rectangle [length, height].
Count the rectangle if length is at least x and height is at least y.
Record the total count for that point.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every rectangle is checked directly against every point, with no precomputation or grouping.
With both rectangles and points up to 100000, this repeats a huge number of redundant comparisons.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rectangles.length times points.length).
Space: O(1) extra beyond the result.
Limitation: with both counts up to 100000, this is up to 10 billion comparisons, far too slow; the small, fixed height range should be exploited instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every rectangle per point is wasteful: the height range is small and fixed (1 to 100), so rectangles can be grouped by height once, and within each group, lengths can be searched efficiently.

How to answer a query using this grouping: for a point (x, y), sum, over every height h from y to 100, how many rectangles at height h have length at least x, found via binary search in each height's sorted length list.

The core idea: group rectangles by height and sort each group's lengths once; for each query, loop over the small range of relevant heights, binary searching within each.

Group rectangles by height, sorting each group's lengths. For each query point (x, y), loop over every height from y up to the maximum possible height, and for each height present, binary search its sorted length list for how many lengths are at least x, summing these counts.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: group by height, binary search lengths within each relevant height

blocks.text: Grouping rectangles by height means every rectangle at a given height with length at least x is exactly what a binary search on that height's sorted length list finds directly. Since a point's y-coordinate only ever needs heights at least y considered, and the height range is capped at 100, looping over that small range and binary searching each relevant group answers every query with far less work than checking every rectangle individually.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) to group and sort once, then O(100 times log n) per query.
Space: O(n) for the grouped structure.

blocks.text: This problem shows how a small, fixed constraint (height capped at 100) can be exploited directly: group by that bounded dimension, and binary search the other, unbounded dimension within each group.

items: Forgetting that "contains" is inclusive of the boundary (length or height exactly equal to the point's coordinate still counts).
Looping over the full possible length range instead of the small height range, missing the key optimization opportunity.

blocks.text: Explicitly noting the small, fixed height range (1 to 100) as the key structural fact enabling this optimization shows attention to the problem's specific constraints, not just its general shape.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "the height is capped at a small number", think: group by height, and binary search the other dimension within each group.

items: How would this change if BOTH dimensions had a large, unbounded range?
How would you support adding new rectangles between queries?
Any problem exploiting a small, fixed constraint on one dimension to group and search efficiently within it.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(rectangles times points) time. The optimized grouped binary-search approach runs in O(n log n) to prepare, plus O(100 log n) per query.

items: Pattern: group by a small, fixed dimension (height); binary search the other, unbounded dimension (length) within each group.
Core Idea: a point is contained exactly when some rectangle has length and height both at least the point's coordinates; sum binary-search counts across the small range of relevant heights.
Time: O(rectangles times points) for the brute force, O(n log n) plus O(100 log n) per query for the optimized approach.
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the small, fixed height range (1 to 100) is the key constraint that enables grouping and efficient searching.
Interview Difficulty: a clean example of exploiting a specific numeric constraint rather than treating both dimensions symmetrically.
One line memory trick: group by height (small range), binary search length within each group.
